claim: Humans in sequential-search tasks usually stop earlier than the optimal rule (undersampling), but lose little reward: about 6% of optimal earnings in the price-search task.
agent_test: Measure whether the agent stops candidate generation or evidence search earlier than a DP-optimal rule on a synthetic sequence task; compare reward at equal tokens.
audit_note: Baumann also found people searched too long at positions 7 and later, so 'usually' stop early is fair but not universal.

claim: The undersampling bias is not universal: it reverses (oversampling, too-high thresholds) with attractive faces, shrinks when every choice is paid by its value, and depends on payoff structure and horizon.
agent_test: Run the agent on search tasks with paid-by-value versus top-rank payoffs and check the bias flips with payoff, not by habit.
audit_note: Both the face-task reversal (Furl, Averbeck, McKay 2019) and the paid-by-value and horizon results (van de Wouw, McKay, Furl 2024) come from the same Furl/McKay group; Goldstein et al. does not address the claim.

claim: Human stopping is well described by a threshold that falls roughly linearly with the share of options left, not by the curved optimal threshold or a cutoff rule; linear thresholds earn nearly as much as optimal.
agent_test: Implement a 3-parameter linear-in-remaining-budget stop threshold for the agent and compare with fixed-N and learned thresholds at equal tokens.

claim: The classic cutoff (skip first r-1, then take the next best-so-far) fits human behaviour poorly in full-information tasks; threshold rules beat cutoff rules.
agent_test: Do not use a 37% explore-then-commit rule for agent stopping when scores are observable; use a score-based threshold.
audit_note: Lee et al. 2004 page could not be opened; claim rests on Baumann et al. and Goldstein et al.

claim: The 1/e rule (win probability 1/e, skip n/e) is optimal for the classic rank-only, win-on-best payoff with known n; in Bearden's variant (iid uniform[0,1] values, payoff equal to the chosen value, told only whether each is best so far) the optimal skip is sqrt(n)-1; goals like low expected rank have staged cutoffs (Chow et al.; Ferguson ch. 2).
agent_test: Do not hard-code 37%. When the agent sees a verifier score, use a value threshold; test sqrt(n) versus n/e skip lengths in a simulated candidate stream.
audit_note: The sqrt(n)-1 skip is Bearden's result for iid uniform[0,1] values where the decision maker learns only whether each is best so far, not cardinal payoffs in general; the value-dependent rule is a separate full-information case.
claim_before_audit: The 1/e rule (win prob 1/e, cutoff n/e) is optimal only for rank-only, win-on-best payoffs with known n; with cardinal payoffs the best skip is about sqrt(n)-1 and the optimal rule is value-dependent, with staged cutoffs for expected-rank goals.

claim: The optimal rule for most costed search problems is a dynamic-programming comparison of stop-now value against expected continuation value; with iid offers and no recall it is a constant reservation value.
agent_test: Compute a reservation score for accepting a candidate from the agent's own score distribution and test versus ad-hoc stopping.
audit_note: Three of four sources are one textbook (Ferguson) and Goldstein et al. only gives the known-distribution threshold table; 'most costed search problems' is a loose generalisation of the textbook cases.

claim: Humans may learn the stopping rule quickly with distribution-free feedback over many games, but earlier and smaller studies found no learning. In LLM agents, a playbook of stopping lessons distilled from 20 prior trajectories raised timely abstention (Llama-3.3-70B 26.7 to 57.4, d05), a rough analogue; no curve over episode count exists.
agent_test: Test whether the agent improves its stop threshold across repeated episodes when given outcome feedback in context; control with no feedback.

claim: Undersampling is best explained by a pessimistic prior about future options rather than cost-to-sample or a cutoff heuristic; cost-to-sample explains individual differences in one fMRI task.
agent_test: Probe whether the agent under-expects later candidates by eliciting its predicted best-of-remaining before it stops.

claim: Sequential stopping rules for self-consistency voting (Adaptive-Consistency, ESC, reliability-weighted voting) cut samples by large factors (up to 7.9x; 33-84% by task) with about 0.2% or less average accuracy loss. Other labs confirm the direction: Blend-ASC 4.8x fewer samples than SC, RL-guided sampling 33-46% fewer samples than ASC at kept accuracy, PETS 55-75% less budget than uniform (d10-d12). Exact OS-Pruner and OptPO figures have no replication (d21).
agent_test: Replace fixed-N majority vote with a Beta/Dirichlet stop at 0.95 confidence; compare accuracy per token on the agent's task set.
audit_note: Minor: PETS figures are 'up to 75% offline, 55% online' on GPQA, written as a 55-75% range; ESC accuracy is 'comparable' rather than a stated 0.2% bound.

claim: Stopping chain-of-thought via answer convergence or learned stop modules saves about 16-60% of tokens with little accuracy loss on easy and medium tasks, but saves little on hard tasks (AIME -6.9% for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with OS-Pruner), and answer-level signals such as confidence and trial-answer consistency fire too early on hard items. An oracle stop at the first correct prefix improved accuracy by up to 21% (measured mainly on multimodal reasoning benchmarks), while practical early stopping mostly cuts verbose overthinking and does not fix harmful overthinking; hidden-state probes lose false-stop control under calibration-to-test shift (about 31-41% false stops vs a 5% target on MiP and MMLU in Xie et al.).
agent_test: Add an answer-convergence stop at each reasoning chunk; stratify by difficulty and track premature-exit rate and tokens at equal accuracy.
audit_note: The oracle-stop gain of up to 21% was measured starting from multimodal benchmarks (language-only results only 'generalize' qualitatively), and the AIME -6.9% is one model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) at the best-AES point.
claim_before_audit: Stopping chain-of-thought via answer convergence or learned stop modules saves 16-60% of tokens with little accuracy loss on easy and medium tasks, but saves little on hard tasks (AIME -6.9%), and shallow answer-consistency signals fire too early on hard items. An oracle stop at the first correct prefix would gain up to 21% accuracy, but practical signals recover mostly token savings (d19); hidden-state probes lose their false-stop control under distribution shift (30-40% false stops vs 5% target, d06).

claim: More thinking can hurt: beyond a moderate budget extra tokens flip correct answers to wrong, and the best stop point varies with difficulty.
agent_test: Measure accuracy versus thinking length per difficulty bin and test an adaptive cap against a uniform cap at equal mean tokens.
audit_note: Direct flip evidence comes from one study (Zhou et al., two 32B models on AIME, 12K-token turn); Liu and Wang and PUMA only corroborate indirectly (overthinking after correct answer).

claim: Adaptive stopping or allocation beats a flat fixed N or fixed token cap at equal total compute in several independent labs, but the gain is large only under tight budgets and small against a well-tuned fixed setting: Kalayci et al. 15-35% fewer generations at the same quality; CLEAR +11.6 points at 256 tokens per query but +1.2 at 2048 (Balanced stream); Blend-ASC 4.8x fewer samples vs 3.75x for oracle fixed allocation. StreamStop gains a few points of success over validation-selected fixed token budgets on WebShop (40.3% vs 35.0%) but at more reasoning tokens per episode, so that comparison is not at equal compute, and the best stopping signal is model-dependent.
agent_test: Run UCB-style threshold stopping on best-of-N with a reward model and compare to the best fixed N at equal tokens.
audit_note: StreamStop's gain (40.3% vs 35.0% success on WebShop) comes with more tokens per episode (2675 vs 1519), so it is not an equal-compute comparison; other numbers (Kalayci 15-35%, CLEAR +11.6 and +1.2, Blend-ASC 4.8x vs 3.75x) check out.
claim_before_audit: Adaptive stopping or allocation beats a flat fixed N or fixed token cap at equal total compute, across independent labs, but the gain is large only under tight budgets and small against a well-tuned fixed setting: Kalayci 15-35% fewer generations; CLEAR +11.6 points at 256 tokens per query but +1.2 at 2048 (d09); StreamStop a few points over tuned fixed budgets, with the best signal model-dependent (d08); Blend-ASC 4.8x vs oracle fixed allocation 3.75x (d11).

claim: Bayesian sequential tests (SPRT) on rollout votes save 15-60% tokens at kept accuracy.
agent_test: Use an SPRT stop on vote streams; check error rates against fixed-N majority.

claim: Learned stop or escalate policies framed as optimal stopping work in real settings: abort of doomed agent episodes (up to 60% fewer tokens at 90% recall), mid-generation escalation (30% less compute at equal accuracy), sales-call quitting (-54% time on failed calls).
agent_test: Train a cheap probe on early agent state to predict failure and abort or escalate; measure tokens saved at fixed recall.

claim: Formal HJB or full-DP stopping controllers do not always beat simple baselines: Di Gioia's real-LLM test scored lower utility than always-retrieve (EM 0.500 vs 0.817, N=60); stop rules alone gave at most 4 viability points; LLM-written stopping policies did not beat Ridge LSMC. New real-LLM evidence points the same way for LLM self-judged stops: agents that call results useless 97-100% of the time still rarely stop (d02), and prompting an LLM to judge stagnation gave loops (+159% tokens) or a 5.0% accuracy loss while a programmatic gate saved up to 39% tokens at no loss (d14).
agent_test: Always include an always-continue and a fixed-N baseline at equal tokens when evaluating a stop rule.
audit_note: Minor: Qian's paper is about LLM-written exercise policies for Bermudan options (not a formal controller), and the 'stop rules alone at most 4 points' comes from Di Gioia's simulated worlds.

claim: Solving the recurring decision once as an MDP controller and letting the LLM fill content beats having the LLM rederive each step (tau2 telecom 29% to 96% with 93% fewer calls), but suggested stops were mostly ignored in a coding task (followed 6.5%).
agent_test: Compare a scripted controller for stop-versus-continue with LLM-judged stop at equal tokens; log how often the model obeys a stop suggestion.

claim: Human stopping is horizon-sensitive: thresholds fall with fewer trials left, shift with the value distribution in the optimal order, and bounds collapse faster under unannounced time pressure. In LLM agents the budget acts mainly as a deadline: 7-8B models answer at the last allowed action and move it when the budget doubles, without stopping on evidence (d03).
agent_test: Give the agent a visible remaining-budget counter and check that its acceptance threshold falls as budget shrinks.
audit_note: Minor: the time-pressure result (Kira et al.) rests on four participants; the PNAS result gives a linear threshold in proportion of nights remaining, which is consistent with 'thresholds fall with fewer trials left'.

claim: No study was found that gives the classic or cardinal secretary problem to language models, so whether LLMs stop too early like humans is untested. The nearest evidence points the other way for failing sources: agents stop too LATE.
agent_test: Run a cardinal secretary task (known distribution, known n, optimal threshold computed) on the agent and record cutoff position and win rate against the computed optimum.

claim: LLM agents recognise that a source is failing (97-100% of results labelled useless) but rarely stop on that judgment; prompt cues, a stated budget or a stated rule change when they stop, not what they stop on. A harness-enforced integration rule (answer after 5 useless results in a row) fixes the link and raises success by +0.026 to +0.097.
agent_test: Compare a model-judged stop with a harness rule on N consecutive no-progress steps, on a task with a source that silently fails, at equal budget.
audit_note: All the specific numbers (97-100% useless, +0.026 to +0.097, budget and rule effects) come from one paper (Zhang et al. 2026, listed as d02 and d03); the only other source (Context Gathering Decision Process) tests a different setting and only loosely corroborates that LLM self-judged stopping is unreliable.

claim: LLMs are optimistic about their own remaining cost: all 20 model-environment pairs in BAGEN underestimate remaining budget more often than they overestimate it, interval coverage after SFT+RL caps at 47%, and acting on an 'impossible' flag saves 28-64% of tokens on failed runs for a 1.6-4.2 point success loss.
agent_test: Have the agent bound its remaining steps at checkpoints and measure coverage and bias against replay.

claim: Stop signals that depend on a trained hidden-state probe lose their false-stop control under distribution shift (30-41% false stops versus a 5% target on out-of-domain sets), while sequential keyword tests with a built-in level stay within 0.75-9%; probes also do not beat a trace-length rule at locating failure. No head-to-head at equal accuracy on hard solvable problems exists.
agent_test: Compare answer-stability, keyword-sequential-test and a length cap at equal accuracy on a hard set, shifting domain between calibration and test.

claim: When thresholds are set as a quantile of the stop score, any order-preserving miscalibration costs nothing; losses come only from order-corrupting noise or from setting the stop reward in absolute terms. Verbalized confidence is concentrated on few values, so absolute cutoffs on it are coarse.
agent_test: Replace an absolute confidence cutoff with a rank quantile set on a held-out set and compare premature-exit rates under injected miscalibration.

claim: An LLM given the prior over option values and the cost explicitly follows the optimal Pandora-style rule far more often (94.0% match vs 23.0% without, Qwen3-8B, 100 examples). This supports writing costs and priors down before choosing the next operator, but no real-task test of Weitzman's index for operator choice exists.
agent_test: Give the agent per-operator cost and expected gain estimates and compare its operator order with a Weitzman-index order on tasks with known costs.

claim: In tool and retrieval agents, a non-LLM stagnation rule (action overlap, no new facts) beats LLM self-assessment of when to stop: the LLM looped (+159% tokens) when conservative or stopped early (-5.0% accuracy) when neutral; the gate saved up to 39% tokens without loss.
agent_test: Add a repeated-query and no-new-fact gate to the agent loop and compare tokens and accuracy with LLM self-judged stopping.

claim: The human 'stop too early' classic result for the secretary problem is known only secondhand here: Bearden (2006) reports subjects ended search earlier than the optimal cutoff and Goldstein et al. (2020) that Seale and Rapoport found no learning. Computed theory shows stopping early is cheap (n=100: 0.3710 optimal vs 0.3504 at a 25% cutoff).
agent_test: Do not cite a percentage for human early stopping; if needed, obtain the Seale and Rapoport and Gilbert and Mosteller texts.
